There has to be something in place that keeps the website from being profitable by exploiting a certain demographic. If not, then the owner/future owner(s) of voat will seek the adapt it to that demographic's point of view, much like what happened with that other website. If there is only one giant crowd of people who think the same thing then there is no chance of real, challenging discussion; only a giant echo chamber.

The problem is a lot of people like echo chambers. It's why blogs became so popular in the early 2000s when everyone bucked against the filter of professional media editors. I remember a colleague beaming about how she didn't want "their filter," and how blogs were so great because she could curate a big list of people who she absolutely agreed with.

Incidentally, she was a women's studies major...

I mean, yeah... I like echo chambers too but theres a point where you feel gluttonous from constantly being told that your experiences and opinions are more important/greater than the others'. Its much more healthy to seek dissenting opinion to dissect rather than stroke your own ego.

For example, I think being trans in the USA sucks, and a lot of time its uncomfortable present as who you know you are amongst people who swear they know otherwise, but not every transperson is ridiculed and beaten every day they walk out of the house; thats merely the picture sjws paint to stroke their own genitals. When this is bounced around over and over in an echo chamber you get crazy people who dont develop the proper skills to argue against opinions that are challenging to them. They either ignore those opinions or lambast them until they are seen as criminal by others. Then they "win".

Its something that the educational system should seek to stop if we want people to grow up who can argue and debate properly.

But is being able to debate actually important? People are so stuck in their beliefs. It took my brother coming out and losing contact with my parents for a couple years for them to stop saying being gay is evil. People hold their views as a part of their identity and when you challenge their views, they feel like you're putting down who they are. People rarely change their minds from debates.

The question is then, is holding views as an identity part of normal human psychology, or is it a cultural thing?

Because if its the latter, then yeah we should probably try to change that for future generations. :/
